title: Lesson 9: Versioning Your Tools and Instructions: Knowing What Changed and Why
description: Versioning your tools and instructions: what a version, baseline, changelog, and rollback are, why a running record of changes is the only reliable way to know what changed and undo it, and how to build a one-line-per-change log.

questions.question: Priya's monthly vendor summary came back wrong: the overdue-deliveries flag was empty and the tone drifted hedged. Per the lesson, what is the most reliable way for her to work out why?
options: Consult her changelog, which records each change with a date and a reason, and trace the broken behavior back to the exact edit that caused it
Rewrite the prompt from scratch so it looks fresh and hope the regenerated output improves
Regenerate the output repeatedly until it happens to come out close to what she wants
Turn the tool off and do the summary by hand from now on without examining the cause
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that a version problem is best diagnosed by evidence: a changelog with dated, reason-based entries turns a guessing game into a lookup. In Priya's case the log showed she had moved the overdue flag into a variable slot, which is why it went missing. Rewriting, regenerating blindly, or abandoning the tool all skip the diagnosis the lesson recommends.

questions.question: Per the lesson, which habit is what makes a rollback possible at all?
options: Never overwriting the version that works: save a known-good baseline and always work on a copy, so any new change can be undone by returning to it
Keeping every edit in one running file so the most recent version replaces the older one every time
Recording only the changes that turned out badly and ignoring the rest
Writing every change without a date so the sequence is shorter and easier to scan
questions.explanation: The lesson says the human translation of Semantic Versioning's 'contents must not be modified' rule is: keep the good version intact and never edit it in place, save the new attempt as a new version so the known-good baseline survives to be rolled back to. Overwriting, recording only failures, and dropping dates all contradict that and make rollback impossible or misleading.

questions.question: A colleague says versioning is a coding practice that does not apply to him because he only works in a chat tool. Based on the lesson, what is the right response?
options: Versioning applies to instructions too, since editing a prompt, toggling a setting, changing the data, or the tool updating are all version changes worth recording
Agree, because versioning can only work for code and has no use for prompts
Tell him versioning matters only when a workflow involves a spreadsheet
Tell him to version only the output the tool produces, never the inputs
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly says versioning applies to instructions, not just code: a rewritten prompt, a changed tool setting, different data pasted in, and the tool itself updating are all version changes, and are exactly what a changelog is for. The other options dismiss or misplace the habit the lesson recommends.
